items.title: Bela Fleck interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, December 7, 2004
items.q: But I mean I play some Bach, and I know what that is, and I’ve never written anything on a level of that complexity or depth.

ctx.x: Right. All right. Well it just depends what you’re comparing it to. Because I mean if you’re listening to great classical music or if you’re listening to different kinds of jazz through different periods or Indian music, our music would be just pretty simple. You know what I mean? So it depends on the context of what you’re comparing it to. I mean if you’re used to listening to jam bands, or just straight ahead bebop just in four-four that’s complex in the soloing, but the rest of it, the structures can be, I…

feels like it’s in four. If we’re looking for an eleven, we want it to feel like it’s in four. We want to find a way to make what seem to be more complex forms feel very natural and comfortable. But that’s something people have been doing for a long time too. So I’m very aware of the overall context of music, the centuries of music or as much of it as I’ve been exposed to and what’s actually new about our group is probably just a combination of things that haven’t come together before. But in terms of reinventing…

I really enjoyed a couple of things on “Live Art” that stuck out. When you nailed — there’s a vocal tune on there, “O Darlin’” and when you nailed that six-eight groove, and then, later on in the CD you start playing a folk song from North Korea. To me that’s like, well this man has heard and absorbed an awful lot of music.
